subject: Science
source: National Curriculum KS2 Science (States of matter; Animals including humans); Drive Science 'Science lower school' (3.5 matter) and KS3 SOW particle theory progression

lessons.title: Solids, liquids and gases
objectives: Compare and group materials as solids, liquids or gases
Describe the properties of each state
Identify examples that are hard to classify

keywords.def: has a fixed shape and a fixed volume
flows and takes the shape of its container
spreads out to fill any container
the amount of space something takes up

starter: Bismillah. Name something that is a solid in your home.
What happens to water when it freezes?
Is air a material? How do you know?

teach.heading: Three states
bullets: Every material can be in a state
teach.note: Use water as the main example: ice, water, steam. Ask what is the same about all three (the material is still water).

teach.heading: Solids
teach.note: Hold up a spoon or toy. Misconception: powders and sand are liquids because they pour. Each grain is a tiny solid.

teach.heading: Liquids and gases
bullets: Liquids flow and take the container shape
teach.note: Safe demo: pour water into cups of different shapes (volume stays the same). Use a plastic bag with air to show gas fills a space and can be squashed.

teach.heading: Tricky materials
bullets: Sand pours but is a solid
Foam has gas trapped in it
teach.note: Discuss and justify decisions. Encourage 'I think ... because ...'. There is no need to give a final answer to every tricky case.

practice: Sort into solid, liquid or gas: milk, brick, oxygen, juice, wood, steam.
Why is sand a solid even though it pours?
Which state can be squashed easily?
independent: Make a table of three columns: solid, liquid, gas. Add four examples to each from your home.
Write a paragraph to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Choose one tricky material and explain which group it fits and why.
exit: Which state has a fixed shape?
Name one gas that is all around us.
lessons.homework: Find ten materials around your home and sort them into solid, liquid or gas.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide picture cards to sort; allow pointing. Stretch: explain why air in a balloon is a gas.

lessons.title: Changes of state: melting and freezing
objectives: Describe melting and freezing
Measure temperature accurately
Know the melting and freezing point of water is 0 degrees Celsius

keywords.def: when a solid turns into a liquid
when a liquid turns into a solid
the temperature at which a solid melts
a tool for measuring temperature

starter: Bismillah. Name the three states of matter.
Give an example of each.
What happens to ice on a warm day?

teach.heading: Melting
teach.note: Show an ice cube video or let children place a safe ice cube on a plate at home. Melting needs heat energy.

teach.heading: Freezing
bullets: It is the reverse of melting
teach.note: Freezing and melting are reversible. Many materials can be reversed (not all changes can; for example, baking a cake).

teach.heading: Temperature
bullets: Different materials have different melting points
teach.note: Show how to read a thermometer. Chocolate melts at a little below body temperature, which is why it melts in your hand. Different materials have different melting points.

teach.heading: Safe investigation
bullets: Predict which ice cube melts first
teach.note: Safe at-home practical: put one ice cube on a metal spoon and one on a plastic spoon; time which melts first. Stay away from hot water; no kettles for children.

practice: At what temperature does water freeze?
Name something that melts when heated.
If ice melts, can it change back to ice? How?
independent: Record results of the ice cube race in a table and draw a bar chart.
Explain in two sentences why an ice cube melts faster on a metal spoon.
Draw a diagram: solid to liquid (melting) and liquid to solid (freezing), with arrows.
exit: What temperature is the freezing point of water?
lessons.homework: Put water in a small container in the freezer (ask a grown-up). Check it after a few hours and record what happens.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a timeline with pictures and the words melting and freezing. Stretch: explain why salt on icy roads helps (it lowers freezing point).

lessons.title: Evaporation and condensation
objectives: Describe evaporation and condensation
Explain that temperature affects the speed of evaporation
Observe condensation and explain what is happening

keywords.def: when a liquid turns into a gas
when a gas turns into a liquid
water as a gas in the air
when a liquid turns into a gas quickly, with bubbles

starter: Bismillah. What is melting?
What is the melting point of ice?
Where does a puddle go on a sunny day?

teach.heading: Evaporation
teach.note: Ask: where did the puddle go? It evaporated into the air as water vapour. Misconception: evaporation only happens at boiling point; it happens at any temperature.

teach.heading: Condensation
bullets: Happens when warm air meets a cold surface
teach.note: Safe demo: a cold glass of water on a warm day gets droplets on the outside. The droplets come from water vapour in the air, not from inside the glass. Common misconception.

teach.heading: Boiling
teach.note: Show a video of a kettle or saucepan. Children must not handle boiling water. Steam is hot water vapour; the white cloud is tiny droplets.

teach.heading: Fair test on drying
bullets: Measure how long they take to dry
teach.note: Safe at-home practical: two wet cloths of the same size, one in sunlight and one in shade. Link to the variables: only change location.

practice: Which is evaporation: ice to water or water to water vapour?
Why do bathroom mirrors steam up?
Why does washing dry faster on a warm, windy day?
independent: Draw a diagram showing evaporation and condensation with arrows and labels.
Write a prediction for the wet cloth test and explain it.
Explain why drops appear on the outside of a cold glass.
exit: Does water evaporate only when it boils? Explain.
lessons.homework: Put a small amount of water in a saucer on a windowsill and mark the level. Check after two days. What happened?
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use arrows and key word cards. Stretch: explain why a lid on a pan stops water vapour escaping.

lessons.title: The water cycle
objectives: Describe the stages of the water cycle
Link evaporation and condensation to the water cycle
Explain why rain is important

keywords.def: the continuous movement of water around the Earth
water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail
water gathering in rivers, lakes and seas
a mass of tiny water droplets in the sky

starter: Bismillah. What is evaporation?
What is condensation?
Where does rain come from?

teach.heading: Evaporation from the sea
teach.note: Start with the Sun's energy. The salt stays behind when seawater evaporates. Ask 'Where does the water go?'

teach.heading: Clouds form
teach.note: Link to condensation on the cold glass. Clouds are not water vapour; they are tiny liquid droplets.

teach.heading: Precipitation and collection
bullets: Droplets join and fall as rain
Rain runs into rivers and seas
teach.note: Rain, snow, sleet, hail. Water runs off and soaks into the ground. Ask 'Is the water new?' (it is the same water recycled over millions of years).

teach.heading: Why it matters
teach.note: Link to Qur'an 21:30 (Allah made every living thing from water) and to the Islamic teaching to use water carefully and not to waste it (Qur'an 7:31 forbids wastefulness).

practice: Put in order: rain falls, water evaporates, clouds form, water collects in the sea.
What does the Sun do in the water cycle?
How does a cloud form?
independent: Draw and label the water cycle with arrows, using the words evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection.
Write a story from a drop of water travelling around the cycle.
Explain why we call it a cycle.
exit: Name the stage when water vapour turns into droplets.
Where does rainwater go after it falls?
lessons.homework: Make a water cycle in a bag: with a grown-up, put a little water in a clear zip bag, tape to a sunny window and watch for a few days. Draw what you see.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a cut-and-stick diagram. Stretch: explain what would happen if there were no Sun.

lessons.title: The human digestive system
objectives: Name the main parts of the digestive system
Describe the job of each part
Order the journey of food through the body

keywords.def: breaking down food so the body can use it
the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach
a muscular bag that churns food with acid
the long tube where nutrients pass into the blood

starter: Bismillah. Name the three states of matter.
What happens to food after we swallow it?
Why do we need to eat?

teach.heading: Why digest food?
teach.note: Use a bread-chewing analogy: bread becomes mush. Digestion is partly physical (chewing) and partly chemical (enzymes), but keep to physical at this level.

teach.heading: Mouth to stomach
teach.note: Swallowing: muscles squeeze food down even if you are upside down. Misconception: food falls down. Use a video or diagram.

teach.heading: Intestines
teach.note: Small intestine is about 6 m long in adults (accurate at around 5 to 7 m). Large intestine is shorter but wider (about 1.5 m).

teach.heading: Model digestion
bullets: Squeeze through tights: nutrients and waste
teach.note: Safe at-home demo: crackers in a sealed zip bag with a little water (mush = stomach) squeezed gently into a clean sock or tights. Use only clean household items; do not eat the result.

practice: Which organ churns food?
Put in order: stomach, mouth, small intestine, oesophagus.
Where are nutrients absorbed into the blood?
independent: Draw the digestive system and label mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine.
Write a sentence for the job of each organ.
Describe the journey of a sandwich through the body.
exit: Where does food go after the mouth?
What is the job of the small intestine?
lessons.homework: Draw a labelled flow diagram of a piece of bread travelling through the digestive system.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled outline and word bank. Stretch: explain why the small intestine is so long.

lessons.title: Teeth and their jobs
objectives: Name the four types of human teeth
Describe the function of each type
Compare teeth of omnivores, herbivores and carnivores

keywords.def: a flat, sharp front tooth for cutting
a pointed tooth for tearing
a wide back tooth for grinding
the hard outer coating of a tooth

starter: Bismillah. Name two parts of the digestive system.
What is the job of the stomach?
How many teeth do you think you have?

teach.heading: Types of teeth
teach.note: Children look at their teeth in a mirror or camera. Adults have 32 teeth; children have 20 baby teeth.

teach.heading: Inside a tooth
bullets: Enamel is the hard outer layer
teach.note: Enamel is the hardest substance in the body. Simple labelled diagram.

teach.heading: Animal teeth
teach.note: Compare a lion, a cow and a human using photos. Link teeth shape to diet.

teach.heading: Caring for teeth
teach.note: Link to the Sunnah of using the miswak and cleanliness as part of faith (Sahih Muslim). Safe demo: put an eggshell in a cup of vinegar and one in water overnight (vinegar is household and safe if not drunk) to model acid and enamel. Use a grown-up.

practice: Which tooth is best for cutting an apple?
Why do herbivores have flat molars?
Which tooth type tears meat?
independent: Draw a diagram of a set of teeth and label the four tooth types.
Compare the teeth of a cow and a lion in a table.
Write three tips for caring for your teeth and explain why each one helps.
exit: Name the tooth type that grinds food.
Why should we limit sugary drinks?
lessons.homework: Keep a record of when you brush your teeth for one week and list the foods you ate that could harm them.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a labelled mouth picture. Stretch: explain what would happen to a cow with sharp canines.

lessons.title: Food chains: producers, predators and prey
objectives: Construct food chains and name producers, consumers, predators and prey
Explain what happens when one organism in a food chain is removed
Use arrows correctly

keywords.def: a plant that makes its own food using sunlight
an animal that eats other living things
an animal that hunts other animals for food
an animal that is hunted by predators

starter: Bismillah. Name the four types of teeth.
What does a herbivore eat?
What does the arrow in a food chain mean?

teach.heading: Start with the Sun
teach.note: All food chains start with a producer. Energy comes from the Sun. Misconception: food chains start with the Sun; the first living thing is the producer.

teach.heading: Consumers
teach.note: Example: grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, hawk. Draw on the board and read with 'is eaten by'.

teach.heading: When one link changes
teach.note: Discuss a pond: if snails die, fish lose food. Link to caring for the environment: Allah has trusted us to look after His creation.

teach.heading: Build chains
teach.note: Children build chains using picture cards. Check arrow direction and that chains begin with a producer.

practice: Name the producer in: grass, rabbit, fox.
Which animal is the predator in: leaf, caterpillar, bird?
What happens to the fox population if rabbits die out?
independent: Draw a four-link food chain for a pond and label the producer, consumers and predator.
Write what would happen if one animal disappeared from your chain.
Create a food chain for a desert using a camel, a plant and one other animal.
exit: What must every food chain begin with?
lessons.homework: Draw a food chain from your garden or local park and explain what would happen if one link were lost.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide picture cards and arrow templates. Stretch: draw a simple food web with two linked chains.

lessons.title: Review and investigation: digestion and diet
objectives: Recall key ideas from digestion, teeth and food chains
Carry out a simple investigation on healthy eating habits
Present results in a table or chart

keywords.def: a test or survey to find something out
information collected, such as numbers
what the results tell us
asking people questions to collect data

starter: Bismillah. Name three parts of the digestive system.
Which teeth do herbivores use for grinding?
Name a producer in a food chain.

teach.heading: Revision map
teach.note: Quick recap using a concept map. Ask children to add one fact each. Correct misconceptions from earlier lessons.

teach.heading: Planning a survey
bullets: Question: how many fruit and vegetable portions do we eat?
teach.note: Children ask five family members, or use the class. Model a clear survey question. Sensitive: do not compare children's family food; keep anonymous.

teach.heading: Presenting data
teach.note: Model how to draw a bar chart with a title, labelled axes and equal intervals. Common error: bars touching or uneven scales.

teach.heading: Drawing conclusions
teach.note: Use sentence starters. Encourage tentative language: 'The data suggest ...'. Link to the Islamic teaching to eat what is good (tayyib) and to thank Allah for food.

practice: Five people ate 2, 4, 1, 3, 5 portions of fruit and vegetables. What is the highest number?
Complete the bar chart title for this data.
What conclusion can we draw if most people eat 2 portions?
independent: Carry out the survey with five people and record your results in a tally table.
Draw a bar chart of your data with a title and labels.
Write a conclusion and one suggestion for healthier eating.
exit: Why do we use a bar chart?
Name one thing you learned about digestion.
lessons.homework: Finish your bar chart and conclusion, then teach a family member one fact about teeth.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a blank chart template and sentence starters. Stretch: calculate the mean number of portions.
